Pacino is an open source 8-issue out-of-order RISC-V processor targeting the RVA23S64 profile. RTL is written in SystemVerilog, simulated with Verilator, and verified with a combination of directed tests, functional coverage, formal analysis via SymbiYosys and riscv-formal, and spike-dasm as an independent oracle. Gate synthesis targets Yosys with FPGA mapping via Quartus and Vivado. Design decisions, AI-assisted co-design records, and architectural rationale are committed alongside the RTL.

docs.title: IA task browser
docs.text:
Anatomy of a task file

Written before the run, by the designer and the PA:

  • Header: task ID, date, module, model, runtime, context used, PA session, task type, mode and status
  • Overview: a short summary
  • Context: the files the IA loads, kept deliberately small
  • Hypothesis: the question the task is asking
  • Background: what the IA, or a human reader, needs to know
  • Binding previous decisions: earlier decisions that apply, which the IA can use to check that the task makes sense
  • Requirements: what the run must deliver
  • Constraints: the limits of the run

Written by the IA, in Results Capture:

  • What was delivered, the test matrix and the test results
  • Assumptions and decisions the IA made where the prompt gave no guidance
  • RVA23 compliance risks and edge behavior
  • Deferred work and other notes
  • Files modified, and a context usage report

Written after the run, in the results discussion: the IA's console output, my assessment and the PA's assessment.

docs.title: Frontend Overview
docs.text:
Pacino implements a 'decoupled frontend' with a branch prediction cluster of 7 predictors feeding an instruction fetch unit, an address translation stage and an instruction decoder which can decode at least 8 instructions per cycle.

This page is an introduction to Pacino's frontend. The discussion walks through the two diagrams below covering the operation of the frontend and coordination between the components.

The design decisions which arrived at this implementation are found in the planning documents pacino/planning/arch. These are linked at the end.

There are waveform views of the principal operations of the frontend. Major behaviors are described here: frontend demonstration.

These pages aim to be readable by newer designers without being tedious for experienced ones; feedback on the level of detail is welcome.

Experienced designers may prefer to go directly to the specs and RTL.

docs.title: A decoupled frontend
docs.text:
In baseline frontends branch prediction and instruction fetch operate in lockstep. The predictor chooses the next address, the instruction cache reads it, and the next prediction waits for the fetch to finish.

Performance of this basic microarchitecture is improved by decoupling portions of the frontend. Pacino implements a decoupled frontend based on a fetch target queue (FTQ).

The branch predictor produces a stream of predicted fetch addresses and writes these to the FTQ. The fetch unit (IFU) processes entries in the FTQ in order as they appear. This weakens the interlock between prediction and fetch/icache access. This organization was introduced by Reinman, Austin and Calder [1].

The FTQ serves another purpose: it provides a look ahead of addresses that fetch will need soon, telling the processor which instruction cache lines to bring in. This mechanism is the basis for fetch-directed prefetching [2]. Pacino's future prefetch mechanism will use this mechanism.

Because an FTQ entry can be corrected after it is written, the FTQ lets a fast, simple predictor start fetch immediately while slower, more accurate predictors perform their look ups. When the slower predictors agree with the fast predictor, cycles of latency are saved [3].

Decoupled frontends of this kind are now standard in high-performance cores; these can be found in public information on commercial designs [4]. The XiangShan series of open source designs also implement decoupled frontends [5].

FTQ management logic uses the state in each entry to assist branch predictor training and to restore processor state on mispredictions. Pacino uses a redirect mechanism so that early start predictions can be corrected when the slower more accurate predictor(s) disagree. A redirect will find and discard every younger entry and each associated in-flight fetch.

Prediction can run ahead only as far as the branch target buffer (BTB) can identify branch locations. On a BTB miss, the branch is not identified, the direction and target predictors are never consulted and the block is predicted to fall through to a default, the ‘fall-through address’. If that branch is taken, the predicted stream, and any prefetching driven by it, continues down the fall-through path until predecode or branch resolution in the backend detects the branch and redirects fetch. Much recent work addresses this limit [6, 7].

docs.title: Pacino’s three pipelines
docs.text:
The frontend is built as three pipelines that run independently:

  1. The prediction pipeline, in the branch prediction cluster (bp_cluster), decides which code comes next.
  2. The translation pipeline, in the instruction fetch unit (IFU) and the instruction TLB, turns each predicted address into a physical address.
  3. The fetch pipeline, in the IFU and the level-one instruction cache (L1I), reads the bytes, finds the instructions in them and passes them on to the instruction buffer and decode.

In Pacino the branch prediction cluster writes predicted blocks into a 64-entry FTQ, and the IFU takes them from the FTQ in order.

The FTQ speculatively uses the prediction available in p1, formed by the micro-BTB (uBTB) and the loop predictor (LP), to allocate the entry and begin fetch. If later predictions disagree, e.g. in p2 or p3 from TAGE or SC, the FTQ entry is corrected and a redirect occurs. Redirects cancel any incorrect pending fetches and start fetches from the corrected (redirected) address.

Pacino also decouples address translation: the instruction TLB works on the FTQ through its own pointer, xlate_ptr, ahead of fetch, so a translation can complete before fetch reaches the block.

This arrangement is the core of Pacino's decoupled frontend. Prediction can run ahead of fetch while fetch is waiting, for example on a cache miss, so the FTQ fills with the addresses fetch will need next. The pipeline view shows this: its two halves are not aligned in time, because they are linked only through the queue.

The FTQ tracks its entries with four pointers, oldest first: commit_ptr (entries the backend has retired), fetch_ptr (the next entry to fetch), xlate_ptr (the next entry to translate) and alloc_ptr (the next entry the prediction pipeline will write).

docs.title: Prediction blocks and slots
docs.text:
In Pacino the unit of prediction is the prediction block: up to 32 bytes of code that begin at any 2-byte address. A block ends at the first branch predicted taken, and the next block begins at that branch's target. One FTQ entry holds one prediction block.

A block can contain more than one branch. Each prediction slot describes one of them, and the compile time parameter NUM_PRED_SLOTS sets how many slots a block has. With two slots, the frontend can predict two branches in one block, so a not-taken branch does not end the block early. When a block holds more branches than it has slots, the block ends at the first branch it cannot describe, and the next block starts with that branch.

The prediction block is not the same as the 64-byte cache line the IFU reads from the L1I. The IFU reads a whole line and extracts the block from it.

docs.title: The prediction pipeline
docs.text:
Prediction takes up to four cycles, p0 to p3. Each stage has its own predictors, and each later stage may correct the earlier answer.

Stage Operation Predictors p0 The FTQ presents the block's start address. Table indices are formed from the address and the branch history. RAS top-of-stack read p1 The initial prediction is formed. The FTQ allocates an entry and fetch can begin. uBTB, loop predictor p2 The block's contents and the main direction and target predictions arrive. FTB, TAGE, ITTAGE, RAS push or pop, loop predictor re-read p3 The statistical corrector gives the final direction. SC

The FTQ never waits for a predictor later than p1. A later stage that disagrees with what the FTQ already holds sends a redirect instead, which rewrites the entry and restarts fetch from the corrected address.

The seven predictors, and the module that keeps the branch history, are:

  • uBTB (micro branch target buffer, 256 entries, 4-way). A small, combinational predictor that gives the first guess at p1.
  • Loop predictor. Learns the trip count of regular loops so that the loop's exit is predicted correctly. It answers at p1 and again at p2.
  • FTB (fetch target buffer, 2048 entries, 4-way). Records, for each block start address, where the block ends and the branches in it: their positions, types and targets. It is the authority on what a block contains.
  • TAGE. The main direction predictor for conditional branches: a base table T0 and four tagged tables, T1 to T4, each of 2048 entries. The tagged tables are indexed by the address combined with 8, 13, 32 and 119 bits of branch history.
  • SC (statistical corrector). Can reverse TAGE's direction at p3 when its own counters disagree strongly.
  • ITTAGE. Predicts the targets of indirect jumps, built like TAGE but storing targets instead of directions.
  • RAS (return address stack). Predicts return addresses. Calls push it and returns pop it.
  • History module (bp_history). Keeps the global branch history (256 bits) that the history-indexed predictors use, and checkpoints it so that it can be restored after a misprediction.

At p2 the FTB will know the branch type. The type decides which predictor supplies the target:

Branch type Target comes from Return RAS Indirect jump ITTAGE Conditional branch The FTB's target if taken, otherwise the next block Direct jump FTB

For conditional branches without a trusted loop prediction, the later-stage predictors are assumed to be more accurate. In order of precedence: SC, TAGE, the FTB, then the uBTB. TAGE and the FTB outputs are valid at p2; TAGE takes precedence over the FTB.

A trusted loop prediction outranks all of these. Once the loop predictor is confident in a loop’s trip count, its p2 direction stands. In this case the SC does not override it at p3.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Three places can redirect fetch:

  1. The prediction pipeline at p2 or p3, when a later predictor corrects the initial prediction.
  2. Predecode, in the IFU, when the bytes fetched contradict the prediction, for example a branch where the prediction assumed none.
  3. The backend, when a branch resolves differently from its prediction.

A redirect names one FTQ entry and one slot. A later stage wins over an earlier stage for the same entry and slot. The younger blocks already in flight are dropped from both IFU pipelines, and fetch restarts from the new address.

The time from a redirect to the first translation request at the new address is short:

Redirect source Cycles to the new translation request p2 or p3 prediction 1 Predecode 2 Backend 2

A backend redirect also clears the IBUF. Prediction redirects do not.

docs.title: Translation and fetch
docs.text:
The translation pipeline takes the entry at xlate_ptr. The ITLB (64 entries, includes PMP and PMA checks) translates the block's start address in one cycle on a hit. A block that crosses a page boundary requires a second lookup in the next cycle. A miss goes to the page table walker (PTW). The resulting physical address with memory attributes or a fault waits in a four-entry queue for fetch.

The fetch pipeline takes the entry at fetch_ptr and runs in four stages:

Stage What happens F0 Accept the request, read the translation, and send zero to two requests to the L1I. F1 Compute the address of every 2-byte position in the block while the cache access is in flight. F2 The cache line returns. Check for faults and select the 17 halfwords that hold the block. (32 bytes, plus 2 for a 32-bit instruction that starts in the last halfword) F3 Expand compressed instructions, predecode, check the prediction, and write the instructions to the instruction buffer.

After F3, a writeback stage reports what predecode found back to the FTQ. This is where the frontend learns, from the bytes themselves, whether the prediction described the block correctly.

The L1I is 64 KiB, 8-way set associative, with 64-byte lines, and returns data two cycles after a request on a hit.

docs.title: Instruction buffer and decode
docs.text:
The instruction buffer (IBUF, 64 entries) accepts up to 16 instructions per cycle from F3 and releases up to 8 from its head. When it is empty, F3's writes pass straight through to the read port.

Decode is eight instructions wide and combinational. It decodes the RVA23 scalar and vector encodings into the internal format the backend consumes.

docs.title: Branch Predictor Training
docs.text:
When the backend resolves a branch, it reports the outcome to the FTQ. The FTQ reads the prediction-time metadata stored with the branch's FTQ entry. This metadata is generated and returned by each predictor with the prediction. The FTQ forms an update for each involved predictor based on branch type:

Branch type Predictors updated Conditional uBTB, loop predictor, FTB, TAGE, SC Indirect uBTB, FTB, ITTAGE Return uBTB, FTB, RAS Direct jump uBTB, FTB Call uBTB, FTB, RAS; an indirect call also ITTAGE

Updates are sent as soon as a branch resolves rather than at retire. TAGE, SC and ITTAGE take updates through a queue in front of their tables, and an update takes two stages, u0 and u1, with single cycle throughput.

A prediction can read a table entry before a pending update to it has been written. That costs some prediction accuracy; in exchange, a prediction is never delayed. The table arbiters always grant predictions first, and an update writes only in a cycle with no prediction presented.

docs.title: The FE Boundary
docs.text:
Three groups of signals cross the fe_top boundary:

  • Backend. Decoded instructions are sent to rename. Branch resolutions, redirects and commits come back to the FTQ, and FENCE.I and cbo.inval come from the commit stage to the IFU.
  • Translation. The instruction TLB's path to the page table walker.
  • Memory. The L1I’s port to the level-two cache.

Some control inputs come from units not yet built: the CSR state, the predictor configuration and the TLB invalidate. The testbenches drive them, and they are the “in:” labels in the block view. The dashed boxes are the testbench models of the backend, the page table walker and memory.

docs.title: Release 01: Frontend Demo
docs.text:
Release fe-0.0.2. The Showcase pages are taken from the release tag fe-0.0.2. The hosted waveforms are published from the same tag; their manifest.json names it.

Twenty-four short programs run on the Pacino frontend, fe_top, with testbench models of the backend, the page table walker and memory. Each scenario shows one behavior: prediction and override, the predictors, redirects, the L1I, translation and faults, compressed code, uncached fetch, cache maintenance, backpressure and commit. Each run ends in a PASS or FAIL line and writes an FST waveform. The Frontend Overview describes the design. How a Scenario Is Built and Run covers the testbench, the program writer and how to read the waveforms.

Select either diagram to open it at full size. The signal annotations on the block view refer to the fe_top connectivity inventory.

docs.title: Scenario Common Description
docs.text:
This document explains the operation of the functions used by the scenarios:

  • the program writer
  • the instruction list
  • the backend model
  • results console status

A glossary of frontend terms is included at the end.

examples/fe_demo/ holds the collateral files used by the scenarios.

Full path Shorthand Explanation examples/fe_demo/docs docs/ demo descriptions examples/fe_demo/programs programs/ scenario drivers examples/fe_demo/tb tb/ demo specific testbench support examples/fe_demo/waves waves/ Surfer signal files

The shared testbench models are found in rtl/core/frontend/fe_top/tb/models/, shortened to models/ below.

docs.title: 1. The scenario
docs.text:
A scenario exercises isolated aspects of the Pacino frontend (FE). The full scenario list is found in planning/showcase/fe_demo_scenarios.md, numbered FD-1 to FD-24. Each scenario has an associated make target in examples/fe_demo/Makefile. The targets are of the form fdNN_<name>.

A scenario has three files, the "program", the wave control file and the writeup:

  • programs/fdNN_<name>.svh
    • contains the task prog_fdNN which populates the models memory and begins exectution.
    • In the demos there is no assembly step, the instructions are written to model memory directly as instruction words.
  • waves/fdNN_<name>.sucl
    • this is Surfer command file: containing signals, groups and markers
    • Events in the waveforms are annotated using these markers. The markers are also described in the scenario description.
  • docs/fdNN_<name>.md
    • the scenario description.

A run has four steps:

  1. begin_scen prints the start line, resets all models and the monitors.
  2. The program task writes the program and the expected instruction list to the model memory.
  3. demo_go releases reset and runs until every expected instruction has retired. The pipeline runs for a number of cycles to allow the pipeline to flush.
  4. The top level evaluates the scenario's correctness and prints the results.

The scenario top level testbench is tb/tb_fe_demo.sv. This testbench instantiates the FE as fe_top, and the page table walker.

The plusarg +SCEN=<name> selects the scenario and run_scen in tb/tb_fe_demo.sv calls its prog_fdNN task.

There are two simulation models, based on the number of prediction slots selected. NUM_PRED_SLOTS selects 1 or 2 prediction slots. Pacino's FE runs either.

NUM_PRED_SLOTS=1 is used for the simpler explanations to reduce amount of data and the number of signals that much be recorded.

Full performance, NUM_PRED_SLOTS=2, scenarios are included to show dual prediction operation. NUM_PRED_SLOTS=2 is configuration used for performance analysis.

FD-3, FD-22, FD-23 and FD-24 run the dual prediction model.

Fast initialization. The predictor tables need an initial value before they can predict. In the design, TAGE, ITTAGE and SC each walk their tables after reset, writing one entry per cycle, and raise a ready when the walk ends: ITTAGE at cyc 513, SC at cyc 1025 and TAGE at cyc 2049 (FD-1). Until all three readies are high, the FTQ holds its p0 request (u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold).

Every scenario except FD-1 skips the walk. The Makefile passes +TAGE_FAST_INIT=1 +ITTAGE_FAST_INIT=1 +SC_FAST_INIT=1 (FE_FAST_INIT, rtl/core/frontend/fe_top/fe_top_srcs.mk). With these, a SystemVerilog initial block in each table writes its initial values at time 0, and each predictor ties its ready to 1 (tage.sv line 333, and the same mux in ittage.sv and sc.sv). Prediction starts on the first cycle after reset instead of about 2048 cycles later.

One effect shows in the waveforms: with the readies 1 from time 0, ftq_pred_val_p0 is already 1 while tb.rstn is low. Nothing captures the request until reset is released, and the first p1 prediction is at cyc 1.

docs.title: 2. The program writer
docs.text:
The program writer builds the memory image and the expected execution list.

The memory image is a byte array indexed by physical address. The expected execution list is the sequence of instructions the program retires, in order. The backend model checks each retired instruction against the list (section 3).

The memory model services instruction cache line requests from the memory image. The page table walker reads from this image.

Scenarios run either in machine mode with physical addresses or in supervisor mode under Sv39 translation. For the Sv39 scenarios, the writer also builds the page tables in the memory image. FD-15 also uses two-stage (guest) translation.

The program writer includes tasks which emit either 16b or 32b instructions. The writer emits either "filler" or "active" instructions.

The filler instructions serve to position an active instruction at a particular PC. The PCs are varied to set up configurations which illustrate operation of the frontend.

The active instructions are branches or jumps, plus fence.i, cbo.inval and a store used in FD-13 and FD-19. Filler instructions are variations of addi. The emitters write filler instructions and branches/etc; demo_go terminates each program with an instruction which jumps to itself, a halt.

The memory image is written before reset is released.

The writer appends each instruction to the expected execution list only if it executes. Instructions skipped by a taken branch are in the memory image but not in the execution list, and a loop appears in the list once per iteration.

Each branch's direction is set by the program when it writes the branch. Register values are never computed (section 3), so a branch's comparison has no effect on its direction: the testbench controls the taken/not taken decision of a branch.

In FD-09 and FD-11 some branch directions are randomized in order to illustrate predictor behavior under those conditions; the testbench uses an LFSR to randomize the taken/not taken state.

docs.title: 3. The expected execution list
docs.text:
The testbench does not model the instruction set. The expected execution list is the reference instead. This list contains the instructions the program retires, in order. The backend model retires an instruction when it matches the next entry (section 4).

Each entry holds the instruction's address and encoding, its control-transfer type, its direction and its target. A fetch fault or a trap the program expects is also an entry. The entry type is ex_t in models/fe_tb_writer.svh.

docs.title: 4. The backend model
docs.text:
The backend is an abstract model. It does not execute instructions. The backend model accepts up to 8 instructions from the frontend via decoder port tb.pd_out and checks these instructions against the expected execution list and retires them in order. The backend model raises tb.dec_ibuf_rdy when it is ready to accept more instructions.

A prediction determines which instruction the frontend fetches after a branch or jump. The model checks the prediction by comparing the next instruction delivered with the next entry in the expected execution list.

If they match, the prediction was correct, and the model reports the branch's outcome, its direction and target, to the FTQ on tb.bkend_ftq_rsv.

If they do not match, the frontend has fetched down the wrong path. The backend model reports the outcome marked as a misprediction, discards the rest of the delivered group, and raises a redirect, tb.bkend_ftq_redir_val, to the expected address. The frontend flushes its younger work and fetches from that address. This is the backend misprediction the scenario descriptions refer to; its cycle is the cycle bkend_ftq_redir_val is high.

The backend model also commits FTQ entries whose instructions have all retired (tb.bkend_ftq_commit_val, tb.bkend_ftq_commit_idx).

Any other mismatch, for example an instruction with the wrong encoding, is a stream error: the model prints a line that begins ERROR: and the run fails (section 5).

The plusarg +TRACE makes the backend print a line for each retired instruction and each misprediction, with the cycle count first. These lines are for debugging and do not follow the result-line format.

docs.title: 5. The result line
docs.text:
To maintain stability in the scenarios, they are developed against tagged versions of the RTL. The Showcase landing page specifies the current tag. The scenarios run internal checks to verify that the waveforms and scenario descriptions match the current state of the design.

A run passes when every expected instruction retires with no stream error and the scenario's checks pass. It writes a result line to its log, out/<scenario>/<scenario>.log, prints one console line, -I: <scenario> : PASS : cyc = <n>, and exits with status 0. Otherwise it writes a failing result line, prints -E: <scenario> : FAIL : cyc = <n> and exits non-zero, which stops make scenarios.

A result line begins with -I: (information), -W: (warning) or -E: (error), then the scenario name. A passing line gives PASS, the counts the checks read, and cyc, the number of cycles from the release of reset to the last retirement:

-I: fd09_tage: PASS, tagged-provider predictions 188, allocations 59,
    T0 by use_alt_on_na 22, cyc 1364

When the expected instructions did not all retire, the failing line says so first:

-E: fd09_tage: FAIL, stream not retired, retired 1200 of 1510,
    stream errors 1, ...

The ERROR: lines for stream errors and the +TRACE debug lines (section 4) use a different format.

docs.title: 6. The cycle counter cyc
docs.text:
tb.cyc counts clock cycles from the release of reset and is shown next to the clock in every waveform.

Scenario descriptions give times as values of cyc. An event "at cyc N" occurs in the clock period in which tb.cyc shows N; a register written in that period shows its new value from cyc N + 1.

docs.title: 7. Reading the waveforms
docs.text:
Each scenario description has an "Open waveform" link that opens the scenario in Surfer in the browser.

From the command line, make view S=<scenario> opens it in a local Surfer session (README.md, section 2).

Surfer shortens signal names to the end of their hierarchical path. The scenario descriptions give the full path in Surfer's form, which names an array element by its index under the array, for example tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.uaon.[0].

A one-slot waveform shows slot 0 of each per-slot signal; a two-slot waveform shows slots 0 and 1. Encoded fields, such as trx_type, are shown as numbers; the descriptions that show one give its encoding.

A scenario whose description has an event table opens with one marker per event, named c<cyc>_<label>, in a group named markers immediately after the clock group, and the view at the first marker. The Events table is section 5 of the description, and section 6 lists the waveform's signals.

docs.title: 8. Glossary
docs.text:
Standard RISC-V terms (Sv39, Sv39x4, VS-stage and G-stage translation, PBMT, PMP, Svadu, link registers) are used as the specifications define them. The entries below give Pacino's parameters, conventions and signal names.

Term Description allocation (TAGE) On a TAGE misprediction of a conditional branch, a new entry is written in the first table with a longer history than the primary's whose entry at the branch's index has an aged useful value of 0. The candidate is chosen at prediction time; if no table qualifies, nothing is allocated. The new entry gets the branch's tag and a CTR of 3'b100. alternate (TAGE) The matching tagged table with the next shorter history below the primary, or T0 when no such table matches. Table number tage_alt_comp in the prediction metadata, 0 for T0. back edge The branch at the end of a loop body that jumps back to the loop's first instruction. It is taken on every iteration but the last, on which it falls through. backend model The testbench's stand-in for the backend (section 4). It retires in program order against the expected execution list, sends resolutions, redirects and commits, and does not execute instructions. block The prediction and fetch unit: at most 32 bytes from a start address, ending at the first predicted-taken control transfer. A 32-bit instruction starting in the last halfword is delivered with the block, which then spans 34 bytes. An FTB entry holds at most one branch per prediction slot; a block with more branches is split at update, ending the entry at the first branch it cannot hold (FD-23). One FTQ entry per block. BPU tb.dut.u_bpu: uBTB, loop predictor, FTB, TAGE, ITTAGE, SC and RAS, and the per-stage logic that combines their predictions. branch type bp_br_type_e, as shown in the waveforms: COND, DIRECT_UNC (jal, rd not a link register), DIRECT_CALL, INDIRECT_CALL (push only), RETURN, RETURN_CALL (jalr with rd and rs1 both link registers and unequal: pop then push), INDIRECT_NONRET and NO_BRANCH. Call and return classification follows the RISC-V link-register hints. bundle Decode's output per cycle, up to eight instructions on tb.pd_out, accepted when tb.dec_ibuf_rdy is high. cbo.inval, fence.i cbo.inval invalidates the cache line holding a given address; fence.i makes earlier stores visible to instruction fetch. At retirement of either, the backend model drives the frontend's commit-stage maintenance port and restarts fetch after the acknowledgment (FD-13, FD-19). commit The backend model raises tb.bkend_ftq_commit_val as its retirement watermark advances; the FTQ commit pointer follows one entry per cycle, freeing entries and committing RAS state for their calls and returns. CTR 3-bit saturating direction counter in tagged TAGE entries, its top bit the prediction: 3'b100 to 3'b111 taken, 3'b000 to 3'b011 not taken. 3'b011 and 3'b100 are weak, 3'b000 and 3'b111 strong. Updates step by one toward the resolved direction. fall through A branch falls through when it is not taken: execution continues at the next instruction. frontend tb.dut: BPU, FTQ, IFU, L1I, instruction buffer and decode. FTB Fetch target buffer: per block start, the block's end and its branches with positions, types and targets. Answers at p2. FTQ Fetch target queue, tb.dut.u_ftq, one entry per predicted block. Issues prediction requests, holds predictions and their metadata, feeds the IFU, and takes resolutions, redirects and commits from the backend. G-stage, VS-stage, two-stage translation Address translation for a guest running under a hypervisor. The VS-stage translates the guest's virtual address to a guest physical address (GPA) using the guest's page tables; the G-stage translates the GPA to a physical address using the hypervisor's Sv39x4 tables. A fault in the G-stage is a guest page fault (FD-15). GPA Guest physical address: an address a guest treats as physical, translated to a physical address by the G-stage. history length T1 to T4 use 8, 13, 32 and 119 branches of global history. IFU tb.dut.u_ifu: translation, L1I access, predecode, and delivery to the instruction buffer. instruction buffer, IBUF The queue between the IFU and decode. ITLB The instruction translation lookaside buffer: it holds recent translations from virtual to physical page numbers for fetch. A miss starts a page table walk. ITTAGE The indirect target predictor, built as TAGE is but storing targets, with its own primary and alternate (ittage_using_primary). Answers at p2. L1I tb.dut.u_l1i, 64-byte lines. Fetches from NC or IO pages are answered from memory as uncached requests (FD-18). LFSR Linear-feedback shift register: a shift register whose input is a combination of its own bits, used for a sequence of bits that looks random. Section 2 describes its use. loop predictor, LP Learns trip counts and predicts the back edge's exit. Answers at p1. misprediction A backend misprediction is a wrong-path fetch detected by the backend model, with a redirect (tb.bkend_ftq_redir_val, cause RC_MISPREDICT). A TAGE misprediction is TAGE's own direction differing from the resolved direction, whatever the final prediction was; TAGE trains and allocates on it. MSHR Miss status holding register: a register in the L1I that tracks one outstanding request to memory until it is answered. override A later prediction stage replacing an earlier one's prediction: FTB or TAGE at p2 (FD-04), SC at p3 (FD-05). It redirects the prediction request stream. p0 to p3 Prediction stages. p0: the FTQ presents a block start. p1: uBTB and loop predictor. p2: FTB, TAGE and ITTAGE. p3: SC. page fault An instruction page fault: translation of the fetch address fails, because a page table entry is invalid or does not permit execute. The fetch traps instead of delivering the instruction. page table walk Reading the page table entries for a virtual address from memory, after an ITLB miss, to find its translation. PBMT Page-based memory type (Svpbmt), a field of a leaf page table entry: normal memory, NC (non-cacheable) or IO. Code fetched from an NC or IO page is fetched uncached (FD-18). position The offset of an instruction from the start of its block, in halfwords: the instruction at the block's start is at position 0, one 6 bytes later at position 3. PPN Physical page number: a physical address without its offset within the page. predecode The IFU's step that finds the instruction boundaries and the control transfers in a block's bytes. prediction metadata Predictor state carried in the FTQ entry from prediction to update. For TAGE: the primary and alternate tables, their counters and directions, the allocation candidate, and whether the primary was the provider; returned as tage_upd_inp_u0[s].tage_pred_meta. prediction slot One branch field of an FTB entry; NUM_PRED_SLOTS (1 or 2) sets how many branches per block are predicted, slot 0 the earliest. TAGE keeps per-slot state, including use_alt_on_na. The demonstration builds a one-slot and a two-slot model (section 1). primary (TAGE) The matching tagged table with the longest history, or T0 when no tagged table matches. Table number tage_prm_comp, counter tage_prm_ctr, direction tage_prm_tkn. provider (TAGE) The table whose prediction TAGE uses: the primary, or the alternate when use_alt_on_na selects it. tage_using_primary is 1 when the primary is the provider. Which of the two provided determines how the update trains the tables. PTE Page table entry: a physical page number and permission bits, or a pointer to the next level of the table. RAS Return address stack with read and write pointers TOSR and TOSW. Each FTQ entry checkpoints them; a redirect restores the RAS from the named entry's checkpoint. redirect Sources: the BPU at p2 and p3, the IFU after predecode, and the backend on a misprediction or trap. resolution tb.bkend_ftq_rsv, one per resolved branch: FTQ index, position, direction, target, type, mispredict flag and instruction length. A conditional's target is its taken target whatever its direction. The FTQ converts resolutions into predictor updates. retire Complete an instruction in program order. In the demonstration the backend model retires an instruction when it matches the next entry of the expected execution list (section 4). SC Statistical corrector; may reverse TAGE's direction at p3. stream error A delivered instruction that does not match the expected execution list and is not explained by a misprediction. It fails the run. Sv39, Sv39x4 RISC-V page table formats. Sv39 translates 39-bit virtual addresses through three levels of tables to 4 KiB pages. Sv39x4 is the G-stage format, which translates 41-bit guest physical addresses. T0, T1 to T4 The TAGE tables: T0 the base table, T1 to T4 the tagged tables in order of increasing history length. tag, tag match A tagged table entry stores a short value formed from the branch address and the history. The entry matches a prediction request when its stored tag equals the request's. TAGE The direction predictor for conditional branches, instance tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage. It has the base table T0 of 2-bit counters, initialized to 2'b10 (weakly taken), and four tagged tables T1 to T4, and answers at p2. tagged table A TAGE table whose entries carry a tag, so an entry answers only for the branch and history that wrote it, as far as the tag can tell them apart. TOSR, TOSW The RAS's top-of-stack read and write pointers. Each FTQ entry holds a copy of them, and a redirect restores the RAS from the copy in the entry it names. trap A transfer of control to a handler on an exception, such as a page fault or an access fault, or on an ecall. trip count The number of iterations a loop runs. uBTB Micro BTB; answers at p1. update A TAGE update arrives on tage_upd_val_u0 with tage_upd_inp_u0 and is written in the cycle trx_type is 1. Update conversion, tb.dut.u_ftq.u_upd_conv, builds each predictor's update input from a resolution and the FTQ entry's metadata. use_alt_on_na uaon, a 4-bit counter per prediction slot. When it is 8 or more and the primary is a tagged table with a weak CTR, the alternate is the provider. It is updated only when the primary and the alternate are both tagged tables. useful counter 2 bits per tagged entry, aged by period: full value in the current period, half in the next, 0 after that (ueff_p1). An entry whose aged value is 0 may be replaced by an allocation. VPN Virtual page number: a virtual address without its offset within the page. weak A CTR value of 3'b011 or 3'b100, the two values nearest the boundary between not taken and taken.

docs.text:
Open waveform

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Scenario fd01_reset_init (FD01) shows the post-reset initialization of the RAMs in the TAGE, ITTAGE and SC. These branch predictor tables require an initial value before they are trained by executed branch behavior.

Initialization is done with simple FSMs that walk the table addresses writing the constants one cycle per entry. There are 2048 TAGE entries, 512 ITTAGE entries and 1024 SC entries. All tables are initialized in parallel.

Ready signals indicate to upstream logic when the predictors have completed this initialization.

This waveform shows ~2048 cycles for completion of the init process. This is followed by ~295 cycles of example requests. Lastly there are ~100 cycles before termination of the scenario.

The RAS (return address stack) initialization is also shown. The RAS init is a simple reset.

This scenario runs in the 1-prediction slot Pacino configuration. The operations are the same in either 1 or 2 prediction slots.

docs.title: 3. The program
docs.text: The program, prog_fd01, is a loop of 128 passes over 7 instructions. It only provides requests after initialization completes, and nothing in the loop depends on the initialization.

docs.title: 4. Operation
docs.text:
Signal paths are as given in section 6. Event numbers refer to section 5.

Reset is deasserted at cyc 0 (event 0). u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold is asserted because the predictors are not ready, so ftq_pred_val_p0 remains deasserted and no prediction request is issued.1

At cyc 1 (event 1) the u_sram_init FSMs of TAGE, ITTAGE and SC enter the INIT state and begin writing at address 0, with state = 2'b10. Each FSM writes one entry per cycle and all three run in parallel. u_bpu.u_ras.ras_rst_done also asserts at cyc 1, because the RAS requires only a reset.

Predictor Write enable Write cycles Entries Write data Ready asserts ITTAGE u_bpu.u_ittage.ri_wr 1 to 512 512 0 bpu_ittage_rdy, cyc 513 SC u_bpu.u_sc.tbl_ri_wr 1 to 1024 1024 0 bpu_sc_ready, cyc 1025 TAGE u_bpu.u_tage.tbl_ri_wr 1 to 2048 2048 T1-T4: 0, T0: 2'b10 bpu_tage_rdy, cyc 2049

waddr increments by one on each write and ends at the last entry of its table. In the cycle after the last write, the FSM enters the DONE state (state = 2'b11), the write enable deasserts and the predictor's ready asserts. ITTAGE and SC are ready at cyc 513 and cyc 1025 (events 2 and 3), and their ready signals remain asserted while TAGE completes.

TAGE has the largest table, so bpu_tage_rdy is the last ready to assert, at cyc 2049 (event 4). u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold deasserts in the same cycle, and the FTQ issues its first prediction request with ftq_pred_pc_p0 = 0x8000_0000. The FTQ accepts the first p1 prediction at cyc 2050 (event 5). The remaining events show the first predictor responses and the end of the run.

docs.title: fd02_steady: Steady-State Prediction and Fetch
docs.text:
Open waveform

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
fd02_steady (FD-2) runs 2 KB of straight-line code. There are no branches, therefore every uBTB lookup will miss. Consequently the p1 prediction address returned is the fall-through address, the lookup PC + 32 bytes returned in p1 on bpu_pred_pft_p1.

In this scenario the FTQ allocates one entry per cycle. The front end reaches steady state at cyc 20, when decode begins delivering eight instructions per cycle.

The simulation executes 513 instructions, 512 addi and the halt jal. Once these instructions have retired the front end fetches for 100 more cycles, and the simulation finishes.

docs.title: 3. The program
docs.text:
Source: programs/fd02_steady.svh, task prog_fd02.

The RESET_VECTOR parameter is 0x8000_0000.

0x8000_0000   addi t0 x 512      32-bit instruction
...           (addi)             2048 bytes in 32B prediction blocks
0x8000_0800   jal x0,0           halt, loop to self

docs.title: 4. Operation
docs.text: Signal paths are as given in section 6. Event numbers refer to section 5.

docs.title: 4.1 Prediction and FTQ allocation
docs.text:
Reset is deasserted at cyc 0 (event 0). No hold condition is active, so ftq_pred_val_p0 is asserted and the FTQ issues its first prediction request, with ftq_pred_pc_p0 = 0x8000_0000 and ftq_pred_idx_p0 = 0.1

The BPU returns the p1 prediction at cyc 1 (event 1), with bpu_pred_val_p1 asserted. The uBTB lookup misses: u_bpu.r_ubtb_blk_p1.hit and bpu_pred_slot_p1.[0].slot_valid are deasserted, and bpu_pred_pft_p1 is the lookup PC + 0x20. u_ftq.w_ok_pred_p1 asserts when bpu_pred_idx_p1 matches the outstanding request, and this writes the prediction into the FTQ entry.2

In the same cycle, bpu_pred_pft_p1 drives ftq_pred_pc_p0 combinationally. This is the zero-bubble path: the next request is presented in the cycle in which the current prediction is formed, so no idle cycle separates consecutive prediction blocks.3 As a result, ftq_pred_pc_p0 increments by 0x20 per cycle and u_ftq.w_ok_pred_p1 remains asserted from cyc 1. u_ftq.u_npc.w_hold, ftq_full, u_ftq.w_ok_slot_p2 and u_ftq.w_ok_slot_p3 remain deasserted throughout.

docs.title: 4.2 Instruction fetch
docs.text:
The FTQ presents entries to the IFU from cyc 3. ftq_ifu_req_val and ftq_ifu_req_rdy are asserted, so one block transfers per cycle, with ftq_ifu_next_pc equal to ftq_ifu_start_pc + 0x20.

Each block fetch covers 34 bytes: the 32-byte block plus one halfword, for a 32-bit instruction that crosses the block end. A block that starts in the upper half of a 64-byte L1I line therefore requires two lines, and it reuses the first if the previous block requested it. Block 0x8000_0000 requests line 0x8000_0000 at cyc 4 and block 0x8000_0020 requests line 0x8000_0040 at cyc 5. Thereafter, only the upper-half blocks issue requests, so ifu_l1i_req_val asserts on odd cycles from cyc 7. l1i_ifu_rsp_val first asserts at cyc 16 and then asserts every second cycle.5

docs.title: 4.3 Delivery to decode
docs.text:
The block at 0x8000_0000 reaches the IBUF at cyc 18 (event 2). ifu_ibuf_val is asserted and u_ibuf.w_n_pres is 8, so all eight tb.pd_out.[i].valid lanes are asserted. tb.dec_ibuf_rdy is asserted, so u_ibuf.w_n_pop is also 8. Each block passes through the IBUF without accumulating, and u_ibuf.r_count remains 0.

No block is delivered at cyc 19, because block 0x8000_0020 also requires line 0x8000_0040, which is returned at cyc 18 and is readable from cyc 19. From cyc 20 (event 3) through cyc 82, one full bundle is delivered every cycle, with tb.pd_out.[0].start_pc incrementing by 0x20. This is the steady state: one line every two cycles, at two blocks per line and eight instructions per block, delivers eight instructions per cycle.

Predecode writes back to the FTQ one cycle after each bundle, with ifu_ftq_pdwb_val asserted and ifu_ftq_cfi_val deasserted until the halt. u_ftq.w_commit_ptr advances one entry per cycle from cyc 23.

docs.title: 4.4 Halt
docs.text:
Prediction continues past the halt JAL, which has not been trained into the BPU. ftq_pred_pc_p0 reaches 0x8000_0800 at cyc 64 and continues along the fall-through path to 0x8000_0a60.

The halt block reaches decode at cyc 83 (event 4). u_ibuf.w_n_pres is 1, so only lane 0 is valid. At cyc 84 the predecode writeback identifies the JAL: ifu_ftq_cfi_val and ifu_ftq_mis_val are asserted, ifu_ftq_mis_pos is 0 and ifu_ftq_target is 0x8000_0800. This asserts u_ftq.w_pd_redir_val, u_ftq.w_redir_val and ftq_ifu_flush_val, and redirects ftq_pred_pc_p0 to 0x8000_0800.

The last instruction has retired by cyc 84 (event 5), so tb.dec_ibuf_rdy deasserts.4

docs.title: fd09_tage: TAGE Provider, Allocation and use_alt_on_na
docs.text:
Open waveform

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Scenario fd09_tage (FD09) shows three behaviors of the Pacino TAGE predictor in response to fetch target queue (FTQ) prediction requests at pipestage p0 and FTQ updates at pipestage u0:

  1. a prediction supplied by a tagged table
  2. the allocation of a new tagged entry after a misprediction
  3. the use_alt_on_na1 mechanism handing a prediction from a weak tagged entry to the base table T0.

FD09 runs a loop whose body contains a conditional branch with a random direction. The random direction is chosen by the program writer class and resolved by the modeled backend. With the random direction the predictor cannot learn the branch behavior and therefore mispredicts often. These mispredictions result in allocations and eventually trigger the use_alt_on_na (UAON) counter. Eventually the UAON counter causes the prediction to use the base table T0 as the prediction source.

Branch predictors and decoupled frontend designs are well-researched. Some of the seminal papers include [1] [2] [3] [4].

Pacino terminology labels the prediction operation stages as p0/p1/etc and the branch predictor update operation stages u0/u1/etc.

This scenario runs in the 1-prediction slot Pacino configuration, NUM_PRED_SLOTS=1, to reduce the volume of signal data.

docs.title: 3. The program
docs.text:
The program is written by the task prog_fd09 in programs/fd09_tage.svh. The code consists of a short prologue, then a 256 iteration loop, and a short epilogue.

The loop body holds two conditional branches. The bne branch at 0x8000_000E has a randomized direction. The bne branch at 0x8000_0016 returns to label top. This is the loop's back edge, labeled BE in the listing below.

The program runs in machine mode with translation off, the addresses are physical. The program starts at the reset vector, RESET_VECTOR = 0x8000_0000 (bp_defines_pkg.sv), and the loop's first instruction, top, is at 0x8000_0008.

                                                         Position in fetch block
Address      Label  Instruction          Purpose         top   ft  dest   BE
0x8000_0000         c.addi a0, 1         ; prologue
0x8000_0002         addi   t0, t0, 1     ; prologue
0x8000_0006         c.addi a0, 1         ; prologue

0x8000_0008  top:   c.addi a0, 1         ; loop body       0
0x8000_000A         addi   t0, t0, 1     ; loop body       1
0x8000_000E  B:     bne    x6, x0, dest  ; random          3
0x8000_0012  ft:    c.addi a0, 1         ; B not taken     5    0
0x8000_0014  dest:  c.addi a0, 1         ; loop body       6    1     0
0x8000_0016  BE:    bne    x6, x0, top   ; back edge      (7)   2     1    0

0x8000_001A         c.addi a0, 1         ; epilogue
0x8000_001C         addi   t0, t0, 1     ; epilogue
0x8000_0020         c.addi a0, 1         ; epilogue
0x8000_0022  hold:  jal    x0, hold      ; termination

A position is the halfword offset of an instruction from the start of its fetch block. The 32-bit instructions take two positions, so the addi at 0x8000_000A covers 1 and 2. The block at top ends at BE once the FTB has split its entry (section 4.2), so BE is at position 7 only before the split. After it, BE is in a fetch block of its own: position 0 at BE, 1 at dest (B taken) and 2 at ft (B resolved not taken). The figure in section 4.2 shows the fetch blocks.

The c.addi and addi instructions do no useful work. Their purpose is to mix 16-bit and 32-bit instructions and to keep both branches away from the start of the fetch block at top: B is at position 3 of that block and BE at position 7.

Since B's direction is randomized the predictor cannot predict its direction. Therefore the bne at B mispredicts often. The mispredictions cause TAGE table entry allocations and train the use_alt_on_na counter.

The direction of each occurrence of B is chosen by the program writer class and resolved by the modeled backend. The register operands play no part in the taken/not taken state.

B is taken on roughly 1 in 8 iterations, 33 of 256 in the simulation. From 0, the first taken iterations are 9, 16, 19, 22, 30 and 31. RISC-V has no branch delay slots: when B is taken, the c.addi at 0x8000_0012 is skipped.

The back edge is taken on iterations 0 to 254 and falls through on iteration 255. Its pattern is regular, and the predictors learn it.

docs.title: 4. Walkthrough
docs.text: Cycle numbers below are events in section 5; each event is a marker in the waveform.

docs.title: 4.1 TAGE structure
docs.text:
Pacino's TAGE implementation uses 5 tables, T0-T4. T0 is the base predictor which is untagged. T1 to T4 are tagged and use direction history in their access address generation and entry matching. The tagged tables use increasing number of history bits (length), 8, 13, 32 and 119, respectively.

T0 holds a 2-bit counter per entry and always produces a prediction.

A tagged table produces a prediction only when its tag matches. Each tagged entry holds a 3-bit prediction counter, CTR, which encodes a predicted direction in its MSB and a confidence value in the lower bits.

The format for entries in tables T1 to T4 is shown below. All four use the same 8-bit tag.4

For the tagged table two predictions are possible, a 'primary' and an 'alternative' prediction. The table with the longest history that matches the tag produces the primary prediction, the next longest matching table is the alternative prediction or T0 when no other tagged table matches.

A prediction moves through four stages, p0 to p3. The FTQ presents the request at p0, TAGE reads its tables at p1 and delivers its prediction at p2. TAGE's first p2 response is at cyc 2. In all the scenarios the statistical corrector (SC) is enabled. SC takes the TAGE p2 output and uses one cycle to deliver its prediction at p3. If the SC prediction is different from the TAGE prediction, the SC prediction is used and the BPU issues a p3 redirect. The FTQ accepts 36 p3 redirects in FD09 (tb.n_redir_p3), and SC decided all of them. The monitor reads TAGE's own prediction and update signals, so SC changes none of the counts below.

docs.title: 4.2 Fetch block layout and update suppression in this run
docs.text:
Each fetch block has NUM_PRED_SLOTS prediction slots. A slot holds one conditional branch of the block, and TAGE predicts, updates and keeps its use_alt_on_na counter separately for each slot. With NUM_PRED_SLOTS = 1 every fetch block has one slot, slot 0, and the per-slot TAGE signals below are indexed [0].

With one slot an FTB entry holds one branch. When the back edge first resolves in the fetch block at top, the FTB splits the entry for top: it keeps B and ends that fetch block at the back edge's address, 0x8000_0016 (the split at update, planning/arch/ftb_decisions.md section 3, at cyc 32). From then on the block at top ends there, and the back edge is the first branch of the next fetch block, which starts at 0x8000_0016 and has its own FTB entry (allocated at cyc 43 and first predicted at cyc 46). After B is taken, fetch continues at 0x8000_0014; after a backend redirect for B not taken, at 0x8000_0012. The back edge is then the first branch of that block. Either way the back edge is in slot 0 of a fetch block of its own, at position 0, 1 or 2, and is predicted and trained with its own metadata. TAGE indexes its tables with the block's start address, so B's entries and the back edge's are separate. Both are in slot 0, so both train the one use_alt_on_na counter.

The loop's fetch blocks, read from the waveform, are shown below.

The back edge's first two resolutions, at cyc 21 and 32, came before the split took effect. Each was in a fetch block whose one slot held another branch, so its TAGE update was suppressed (rsv_plc_occ, rtl/core/frontend/ftq/rtl/ftq_resolve.sv lines 46 to 57 and 443). TAGE takes 254 updates for the back edge, one for each of its other resolutions, and 256 for B.

docs.title: 4.3 Allocation
docs.text:
TAGE trains on its own prediction, whatever direction the front end finally used. When a conditional branch resolves, the FTQ's update conversion compares the TAGE direction carried with the branch with the resolved direction, and marks a TAGE misprediction when they differ. On a TAGE misprediction, when the provider is not T4, TAGE writes a new entry for the branch in a table with a longer history than the provider's. The table was chosen when the branch was predicted: the first longer-history table whose entry at the branch's index has an aged useful counter2 of 0. The new entry holds the branch's tag and starts at CTR 3'b100, the weakest taken value.

T0's entries start at 2'b10, weakly taken, so until T0 has learned B, TAGE predicts B taken. The first allocation is at cyc 20, for B on iteration 0: B was not taken and T0 had predicted it taken. The allocation comes from TAGE's misprediction alone; the backend's first misprediction, at cyc 21, is the back edge's.

Over the run TAGE mispredicted B on 58 of the 256 iterations: on 31 of the 33 iterations on which B was taken, and on 27 of the 223 on which it was not. Each of the 58 wrote an allocation. TAGE mispredicted the back edge once, when it fell through on iteration 255 (cyc 1355), and that wrote the 59th allocation. The allocations by table:

             T1   T2   T3   T4   total
B            11   12   28    7      58
back edge     1    0    0    0       1

The first taken B is on iteration 9. In the waveform, the backend resolves it at cyc 72: tb.bkend_ftq_redir_val is 1 and tb.bkend_ftq_redir_pc is 0x8000_0014, B's target, because the front end fetched the fall-through. The allocation write is the next cycle, cyc 73, in the tage_update group:

  • tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.trx_type is 1 and tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.tage_upd_val_u0 is 1: the TAGE tables take an update this cycle. trx_type is an encoded field, 0 for a prediction cycle and 1 for an update cycle: it is the arbiter's grant (tage_arb.sv line 76), an input of tage_cntrl.sv (line 58), and the encoding is stated at rtl/core/frontend/bpu/rtl/bp_structs_pkg.sv line 314;
  • tb.dut.u_ftq.u_upd_conv.lp_upd_p0.[0].pc is 0x8000_000E, B's address (the TAGE update input has no address; the update conversion forms every predictor's update from one record, and the loop predictor's copy carries it);
  • tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.tage_upd_inp_u0.[0].cond_mispredict is 1 and .resolved_taken is 1; .tage_pred_meta.tage_prm_comp is 0, so T0 was the provider;
  • tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.u_alc_wr.[0] is 1 and tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.u_alc_comp.[0] is 1: the new entry is written into T1.

RTL: the TAGE misprediction is cond_mispredict, set in rtl/core/frontend/ftq/rtl/ftq_upd_conv.sv line 218. The candidate table is chosen at p1 in pred_logic, rtl/core/frontend/bpu/rtl/tage_cntrl.sv lines 574 to 585. The allocation is formed by alc_upd_comb in tage_cntrl.sv line 853, signal u_alc_wr. T0's starting value is TAGE_T0_SRAM_INIT_VALUE, rtl/core/frontend/bpu/rtl/bp_defines_pkg.sv line 418.

docs.title: 4.4 Training the use_alt_on_na counter
docs.text:
TAGE keeps a 4-bit counter, uaon, for each prediction slot. With one slot there is one counter, tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.uaon.[0]. It measures whether, when the provider's CTR is weak, the alternate has been more accurate than the provider. The rules are in planning/arch/tage_cntrl_uaon_update_rules.md: on an update whose prediction was weak, the counter increments when the provider was wrong and the alternate right, and decrements when the provider was right and the alternate wrong. It starts at 0.

uaon is updated only when both the provider and the alternate are tagged tables. When the alternate is T0, uaon is unchanged. The counter is therefore trained on predictions where two tagged tables matched. B and the back edge both update slot 0, so both could train the one counter; in this run only B's updates do. The back edge's predictions come from T0 until its single allocation on the last iteration, so none of its updates has a tagged provider.

The first prediction from a tagged table is at cyc 115. The history leading up to B is random, so the entries allocated for B are later matched under histories they were not trained on. Those entries are still weak, at CTR 3'b011 or 3'b100, and some predict taken for a branch taken only one time in eight. The table counts the updates that had a tagged provider, a tagged alternate and a weak prediction, by the provider and alternate tables and by what the update did to uaon. It increments when the provider was wrong and the alternate right, decrements when the provider was right and the alternate wrong, and is unchanged when the two predicted the same direction.

             T2 over T1   T3 over T2   increment   decrement   unchanged
B                    16            6          13           0           9
back edge             0            0           0           0           0
The update inputs are in the tage_update group: tage_upd_inp_u0.[0].tage_pred_meta.tage_prm_comp, .tage_alt_comp, .tage_pred_weak, .tage_prm_tkn and .tage_alt_tkn under tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.

In the waveform, uaon.[0] first reads 1 at cyc 225, the cycle of B's update with provider T2, predicting taken, and alternate T1, predicting not taken, weak; B was not taken, so the provider was wrong and the alternate right. No update decrements it. It reaches 8 at cyc 441 and its highest value, 13, at cyc 1031, below the counter's maximum of 15.

RTL: the update is uaon_upd_ff in tage_cntrl.sv line 380, and the condition that both tables are tagged is at lines 383 and 384 (u_prm_tagged and u_alt_tagged, defined at lines 670 and 671).

docs.title: 4.5 T0 provides through use_alt_on_na
docs.text:
When uaon reaches 8, its top bit is set. From then on, a prediction whose provider is a tagged table with a weak CTR uses the alternate instead of the provider. When no second tagged table matched, the alternate is T0, and the prediction comes from T0.

The counter that allows T0 to provide is trained only on predictions where the alternate was a tagged table, as section 4.4 describes. It then governs predictions where the alternate is T0. This follows the update rule in tage_cntrl_uaon_update_rules.md.

In the waveform, the first prediction from T0 through use_alt_on_na is at cyc 460, in slot 0, for the fetch block at top. In the tage_p2 group, tb.dut.u_bpu.u_tage.u_tage_cntrl.tage_pred_meta_p2.[0].tage_prm_comp is 1 (T1 matched B) and .tage_prm_ctr is 3'b100, weak; .tage_using_primary is 0 and .tage_alt_comp is 0, so the prediction is T0's, not taken. All 22 such predictions in the run have T1 as the provider, and all are TAGE answers for the block at top. The monitor counts TAGE answers whether or not the FTQ accepts the group, so a count can include an answer for a block on a wrong path.

RTL: the selection is in pred_logic in tage_cntrl.sv: the trigger, a tagged provider with a weak CTR, at lines 529 to 533, and the choice of the alternate when the trigger is set and uaon[s][3] is 1 at line 539. The result is registered into tage_pred_meta_p2 by meta_p2_ff at line 364.

Runs Surfer in the browser, with nothing to install. The signal setup takes a few seconds to apply.

Run it from examples/fe_demo/: make fd09_tage runs the scenario; make view S=fd09_tage opens its waveform in Surfer.

Source of this page on GitHub

  1. use_alt_on_na: use the alternate prediction table when the provider entry is newly allocated [1]. Pacino treats a provider entry with a weak CTR as newly allocated (section 4.5). ↩

  2. The useful counter USE is aged by the entry's epoch field EPC (see the entry format in section 4.1). Aging is disabled in every scenario: CSR 0x7C0 bit 2, tage_enable_aging, resets to 0 and no scenario sets it, so the epoch stays 0 and the aged useful counter equals USE. ↩

  3. FD09 runs with fast initialization, as every scenario but FD-1 does: a SystemVerilog initial block seeds each predictor table at time 0 and each predictor ties its ready to 1 (tage.sv line 333, the same in ittage.sv and sc.sv), so the table walks of FD-1 do not run. With the readies already 1, ftq_pred_val_p0 is 1 while tb.rstn is still low; the request is captured on the first cycle after reset. The common description describes fast initialization. ↩

  4. The Pacino TAGE design uses a consistent tag width for tables T1-T4, as in Seznec and Michaud's TAGE paper [1]. Other designs have used variable-width tag fields [2]. During performance analysis the benefits of variable-width tag fields will be evaluated. ↩

4. The fe_top boundary
docs.text:
The ports are declared at fe_top.sv:96-217 and grouped as FE-17 (planning/arch/fe_decisions.md:1378) and FE-20 (planning/arch/fe_decisions.md:1445) group them; fe_top.sv:29-60 restates the grouping. -> is a fe_top input read by an instance input; <- is a fe_top output driven by an instance output.

FE-17 counts two groups that cross (translation and backend) and says the instruction path is not a boundary group: what crosses is the L1I's l2-side port mem, a topology edge. FE-20 adds three inward groups (csr, config, maintenance) and one outward dependency, the ibuf read ready. The RTL carries all of them as fe_top ports; the L1I's mem port is section 4.8. Two outputs are in no group (section 4.12).

bkend_ftq_redir_val is the one fe_top net with two readers: the FTQ and the ibuf clear (fe_top.sv:44-45, IBUF-13).

Its members drive existing instance ports by member select (fe_top.sv:52-59, CSR-6): see section 4.10. sc_enable is the one member with two readers, the cluster and the FTQ (fe_top.sv:486, 561; FE-20 config, planning/arch/fe_decisions.md:1459). fe_csr (fe_csr_t, csr_pkg.sv:236-247) is passed whole to the ITLB (fe_top.sv:788).

docs.title: 6. Inside bp_cluster
docs.text: The cluster is a four-stage pipeline (p0 to p3) with an update stage u0 and its write u1 (bp_cluster.sv:55-61). The FTQ-facing ports are grouped in the port list as follows; the predictor instances are at bp_cluster.sv:1812-2035.

docs.title: 6.1 bp_cluster port groups
docs.text:

P0  prediction request, FTQ -> BPU          bp_cluster.sv:109-112
                                            ftq_bpu 3
P1  initial prediction, BPU -> FTQ          :114-123   ftq_bpu 4
RD  redirects p2, p3                        :125-131   ftq_bpu 6
SL  slot correction p2, p3                  :133-150   ftq_bpu 4a
BK  block-scalar correction p2              :152-160   ftq_bpu 4c

ftq_bpu is planning/interfaces/ftq_bpu_interfaces.md.

docs.title: 7. The walker beside fe_top in the testbench
docs.text:
fe_top has no walker; the testbench instantiates one beside it (FE-17 translation, planning/arch/fe_decisions.md:1391; MMU-1a). The shared model rtl/core/frontend/fe_top/tb/models/fe_tb_dut.svh holds both, included in module tb by examples/fe_demo/tb/tb_fe_demo.sv:57 and by tb_fe_top.

fe_top dut (.*)     fe_tb_dut.svh:101  every fe_top port, by name, to
                                       the tb nets of lines 27-99
ptw u_ptw (.*)      fe_tb_dut.svh:122  rtl/mmu/ptw/rtl/ptw.sv:155

What connects them, all by .* name matching:

translation group (itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md 2)
  tb nets fe_tb_dut.svh:45-61 and 106-107
  dut.itlb_l2t_*  (fe_top.sv:143-151)  -> u_ptw ports ptw.sv:170-178
  u_ptw.l2t_itlb_* (ptw.sv:179-188)   -> dut ports fe_top.sv:152-161
walker memory port (planning/interfaces/ptw_mem_interfaces.md 3)
  tb nets fe_tb_dut.svh:108-116
  u_ptw.ptw_mem_req_* (ptw.sv:191-196) -> memory model
  memory model -> u_ptw.mem_ptw_rsp_* (ptw.sv:197-199)
  model: fe_tb_mem.svh:106-226 (initial ptw_mem at 155; ready
  pattern at 224)
walker CSR group (MMU-24a)
  ptw_csr  fe_tb_dut.svh:117 -> u_ptw.ptw_csr ptw.sv:206
  driven by csr_sync, fe_tb_csr.svh:29 (csr_tb_pkg::pack_ptw_csr)
the L1I mem link (section 4.8)
  answered by the same memory model, fe_tb_mem.svh:35-103
  (a_ready at 35, the D-channel responder initial tl_mem at 37)

The walker and the L1I read one memory image (fe_tb_mem.svh; FE-21, planning/arch/fe_decisions.md:1490, ptw_mem_interfaces.md WM-10, line 143). fe_csr and ptw_csr are packed from the one csr_tb_pkg shadow (fe_tb_dut.svh:119-121).

docs.title: 8. Disagreements between the RTL and the planning documents
docs.text:
The RTL is what sections 2 to 7 record.

D1  FTB update port count.
    RTL: 15 payload ports plus the valid (fe_top.sv:274-289;
    bp_cluster.sv:195-211). The comments fe_top.sv:69, fe_top.sv:273,
    bp_cluster.sv:194 and ftq.sv:200 say 14.
    Plan: ftq_bpu_interfaces.md 8 says 15 (lines 883, 895-900; "This
    read 14"). The plan agrees with the ports; the four RTL comments
    are stale since BP-121 added ftb_upd_jmp_rvc_u0.

D2  ITTAGE update payload name.
    RTL: ittage_upd_inp_u0 (fe_top.sv:298; bp_cluster.sv:219-220;
    ftq port bound at fe_top.sv:568).
    Plan: ftq_bpu_interfaces.md 8 table, line 885, "ittage_upd_inp".

D3  TAGE and ITTAGE queue status port names (TD#49).
    RTL: tage.sv:47-48 and ittage.sv:46-47 declare <p>_pq_not_full and
    <p>_uq_not_full; bp_cluster.sv:1945-1946 and 1968-1969 bind them;
    bp_cluster.sv:286-288 says TD#49 was applied by BP-132.
    Plan: ftq_bpu_interfaces.md 8, lines 947-956, says tage and
    ittage declare pq_not_full and upd_rdy without prefix and that
    TD#49 is not yet applied. The cluster boundary names (tage_upd_rdy,
    ittage_upd_rdy) agree with lines 938-939.

D4  uBTB update port at the cluster boundary.
    RTL: ubtb_upd_u0, ubtb_upd_t [NUM_PRED_SLOTS-1:0], 352 bits
    (bp_cluster.sv:186; fe_top.sv:292).
    Plan: ftq_bpu_interfaces.md 8 (line 881) names only the predictor
    port upd_u0; no planning document names the boundary port.

D5  Observation outputs.
    RTL: ftq_full and ftq_empty are fe_top outputs (fe_top.sv:212-216).
    Plan: in no FE-17 or FE-20 group (fe_decisions.md:1378, 1445) and
    named by no interface document.

D6  Decode outputs.
    RTL: decode_bundle, vec_decode_bundle, is_vector, pd_out,
    vtype_hazard (fe_top.sv:103-107), from u_dec (fe_top.sv:820-824).
    Plan: FE-17 backend (fe_decisions.md:1410) says "decode to rename
    and dispatch" with no port list; no interface document names
    decode_bundle, vec_decode_bundle or pd_out (is_vector and
    vtype_hazard appear in dcd_decisions.md:612 and 262).

D7  The instruction group.
    RTL: fe_top.sv:30-32 lists "instruction" as a boundary group, the
    20 l1i_mem_* ports (fe_top.sv:167-186).
    Plan: FE-17 (fe_decisions.md:1378, 1385) counts two groups and
    says the instruction path is not a boundary group, its `mem` port
    being a topology edge; FE-21 (fe_decisions.md:1479, 1490) says the
    port leaves the top as a boundary edge. The ports are the same;
    the documents count them differently.

D8  The config group comment.
    RTL: fe_top.sv:52-54 says "see Results Capture for the ones FE-20
    does not list".
    Plan: FE-20 config (fe_decisions.md:1459-1468) now lists every
    member fe_top distributes (sc_enable, ftb_fastpath_en, the four
    aging inputs, ext_enable); the comment refers to the text before
    the BP-118 correction.

D9  Walker-side labels.
    RTL: the server of the translation group is the page table walker
    (fe_tb_dut.svh:122; fe_top.sv:33-36).
    Plan: itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md 2 (lines 44-63) labels the far end
    "L2TLB" while its line 22 says the server is the walker. Naming
    only; ports and widths agree.

No width disagreement was found: every port width in ftq_bpu_interfaces.md 3 and 8, ftq_ifu_interfaces.md 4 to 6, l1i_ifu_interfaces.md 4.1, 5.1, 10.1 and 11.2, itlb_ifu_interfaces.md 2, ifu_ibuf_interfaces.md 2, ftq_backend_interfaces.md 4 to 6, itlb_l2tlb_interfaces.md 2 and ptw_mem_interfaces.md 3 that was compared resolves to the elaborated width recorded here.
